planting.note: Sow seed in fall for natural cold stratification, or set out conservation-propagated divisions in spring into a lean, gritty, humus-rich crevice mix in full sun to light shade; never collect from wild populations, which are federally protected and confined to a handful of high peaks.

directions: Spreading avens forms a tight basal rosette of rounded, toothed, strawberry-like leaves clinging to shallow soil pockets on exposed cliffs and boulder fields above roughly 5,000 feet in the Blue Ridge, sending up short stems topped with bright yellow, saucer-shaped flowers from early summer into fall. It is a federally endangered cliff-and-outcrop specialist restricted to a few summits such as Grandfather Mountain and Roan Mountain, where it grows at the ragged edge of the spruce-fir zone in thin, gritty, well-drained soil that stays cool and evenly moist from fog and seepage. Gardeners encounter it only through nursery-propagated stock from botanical-garden conservation collections, grown in a crevice garden or trough that mimics the sharp drainage and cool root zone of its rock-ledge habitat; it resists heat and humidity poorly and should never be planted where runoff or rich garden soil collects around the crown.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Recovery Plan

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock from regional native-plant growers in fall or early spring into cool, rocky, humus-rich soil in the dappled light of a spruce-fir opening or rock-ledge margin; this high-elevation endemic needs consistently cool summer soil and resents being moved into lowland heat.

directions: Skunk goldenrod takes its unusual common name from the pungent, resinous smell released when its broad, toothed leaves are bruised, a trait that distinguishes it in the field from the many other goldenrods sharing the Southern Blue Ridge high peaks. Solidago glomerata is a rhizomatous perennial confined to rock outcrops, cliff edges, and the thin, mossy clearings within red spruce-Fraser fir forest above about 5,500 feet on mountains such as Mitchell, Roan, and the Black Mountains, where it produces tight, clustered heads of small yellow flowers in late summer against the cool backdrop of conifer shade. It is grown only by specialty native-plant nurseries and botanical-garden propagation programs working with regional high-elevation ecotypes, and it performs best in a shaded rock garden or spruce-fir companion planting that keeps roots cool and evenly moist through the growing season. Divide congested clumps every few years in fall to maintain vigor, and avoid hot, dry, or heavily fertilized sites.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall for cold stratification, or plant small divisions from alpine/rock-garden specialty growers into a lean, gritty, sharply drained crevice or trough mix in full sun; it needs cool roots and will not tolerate rich, water-retentive garden soil.

directions: Mountain sandwort forms a tiny, wiry-stemmed cushion of narrow, needle-like leaves studded in summer with small, five-petaled white flowers, hugging bare rock crevices and gravelly summit outcrops on the handful of Southern Appalachian peaks that reach into the spruce-fir zone, including Roan Mountain and Grandfather Mountain. It is one of the striking disjunct arctic-alpine species stranded on these high summits since the last glaciation, and it shares the same cold-adapted, wind-exposed, nutrient-poor habitat preference as its relatives on New England's alpine peaks and the far north. In cultivation it belongs in a crevice garden, scree bed, or alpine trough with sharp drainage and cool subsoil, grown from seed obtained through rock-garden society seed exchanges since it is essentially unknown in mainstream nursery trade. Keep it lean and gritty; overly fertile or moisture-retentive soil quickly rots the crown.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs from Appalachian native-plant specialty growers in fall or early spring into cool, rocky, humus-rich soil in the dappled shade of a high-elevation woodland edge or spruce-fir ecotone; keep away from white pine stands where local blister-rust regulations restrict Ribes planting.

directions: Appalachian gooseberry is a slender, sparsely thorned native shrub of rocky woods, ledges, and cool forest margins from New England south through the high spine of the Appalachians into North Carolina and Tennessee, where it reaches its upper elevational limit near the transition into red spruce-Fraser fir forest. Small greenish-purple, bell-shaped flowers open in late spring and are followed by round, bristly, reddish-purple berries with the characteristic sweet-tart gooseberry flavor, borne in modest quantity compared with cultivated gooseberry selections. It tolerates partial shade better than most fruiting Ribes and is valued in native plantings for cool woodland edges rather than for heavy fruit production, pairing well with rhododendron and mountain laurel in an Appalachian understory planting. Prune out the oldest canes every few years to encourage new fruiting wood and good air circulation.

subcategory: high-elevation Appalachian bog and seep shrub

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in consistently wet to saturated, acidic, peaty soil in partial shade, mimicking the high-elevation seep and bog margins where this rare holly grows alongside red spruce; source stock only from specialty native-plant conservation growers.

directions: Long-stalked holly is a deciduous-leaning, loosely branched shrub restricted to a scattering of high-elevation bogs and seepy forest openings in the central and southern Appalachians, often rooted in sphagnum-rich soil within or at the edge of red spruce stands above 3,500 feet. Its small, finely toothed leaves and inconspicuous spring flowers give way to bright red berries on unusually long, slender stalks (the trait behind both its scientific and common names), providing fall and winter food for birds in habitats where few other hollies persist. Because its wild populations are few, scattered, and considered significantly rare, garden stock comes only from botanical-garden and native-plant-society propagation programs rather than general nursery trade, and it must be sited in a permanently moist, boggy, or seep-fed spot in part shade to thrive. It makes an unusual addition to a native bog garden or rain garden in cool mountain climates but fails quickly in average, well-drained garden soil.

subcategory: high-elevation Appalachian seep and spring-head herb

planting.note: Plant divisions from regional native-plant specialty growers in spring into constantly wet, cool, humus-rich soil at a seep, spring head, or streamlet edge in shade; it needs year-round saturated soil and the cool root temperatures typical of spruce-fir seepage zones.

directions: Mountain bittercress is a small, tender-leaved perennial of the wettest microhabitats within Southern Appalachian spruce-fir and adjacent northern hardwood forest, forming loose colonies of rounded, scalloped leaves along the saturated moss and liverwort mats of spring heads, seeps, and trickling streamlets at high elevation. Clusters of small white four-petaled flowers appear in late spring just above the foliage, typical of the mustard family, and the plant spreads slowly by shallow rhizomes rather than aggressive seeding. Because it depends on constant soil saturation and the cool, shaded conditions of a high-elevation seep, it is offered only occasionally by regional native-plant specialty growers and native plant society sales rather than general retail nurseries, and it is best used at the edge of a shaded rain garden, bog trough, or man-made seep feature in a cool mountain climate. It declines quickly if the soil is allowed to dry even briefly during the growing season.
sources: Flora of the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia (Weakley)
